contenido: 1. The one Church of Christ There is only one Church that “our Savior left in the pastoral care of Peter, after the Resurrection (cf. Jn 21:17); To him and the other apostles he entrusted its diffusion and its government (cf. Mt 18:18ff) and erected it as a pillar and foundation of the truth forever” (cf. 1 Tim 3:15); and this Church of Christ, "constituted and ordered in this world as a society, subsists in the Catholic Church, governed by the successor of Peter and by the Bishops in communion with him"[3]. This declaration of the Second Vatican Council is illustrated by the Council itself, when it states that "only through the Catholic Church of Christ, which is the universal instrument of salvation, can the total plenitude of the means of salvation be achieved"[4]; and that the Catholic Church itself "is enriched with all the truth divinely revealed and with all the means of grace"[5], with which Christ wanted to provide his messianic community. This does not prevent the Church, during its earthly pilgrimage, "by enclosing sinners in its own bosom, from being at the same time holy and in need of continuous purification"[6]; nor that "outside its structure", specifically in the Churches or ecclesial communities that are not in perfect communion with the Catholic Church, "numerous elements of holiness and truth are found that, as goods proper to the Church of Christ, drive towards Catholic unity"[7]. Therefore, “it is necessary for Catholics to joyfully recognize and appreciate the genuinely Christian values, coming from the common heritage, found among separated brothers”[8]; and, in a common effort of purification and renewal, they strive to reestablish the unity of all Christians[9] so that the will of Christ is fulfilled and the division of Christians ceases to be an obstacle to the proclamation of the Gospel in the world[10]. But, at the same time, Catholics are obliged to profess that they belong, by a merciful gift of God, to the Church founded by Christ and guided by the successors of Peter and the other Apostles, in whom the original institution and doctrine of the apostolic community persists intact and alive, which constitutes the perennial heritage of truth and holiness of the Church itself[11]. Therefore, the faithful cannot imagine the Church of Christ as if it were nothing more than a sum - certainly divided, although in some sense one - of Churches and ecclesial communities; and they are in no way free to affirm that the Church of Christ today no longer truly subsists anywhere, so that it must be considered a goal towards which all Churches and communities must strive.

2. The infallibility of the universal Church "God graciously arranged that what he had revealed for the salvation of all nations should be preserved in its entirety forever"[12]. That is why he entrusted to the Church the treasure of the word of God, to whose preservation, deepening and application to life the Pastors and the Holy People jointly contribute[13]. God himself, absolutely infallible, has wanted to provide his new People, which is the Church, with a certain participated infallibility, which is limited to the field of faith and customs, which acts when the entire people upholds, without hesitation, some doctrinal element belonging to these fields; and that constantly depends on the wise providence and the anointing of grace of the Holy Spirit, which leads the Church to full truth until the glorious coming of the Lord[14]. Regarding this infallibility of the People of God, the Second Vatican Council declares: "The universality of the faithful, who have the anointing of the Holy Spirit (cf. 1 Jn 2,20,27), cannot be mistaken when they believe and manifest this peculiar prerogative of theirs through the supernatural sense of faith of the entire people when "from the Bishops to the last lay faithful" (Saint Augustine, De praedestinatione Sanctorum, 14,27) They give their universal consent in matters of faith and customs»[15]. However, the Holy Spirit illuminates and sustains the People of God as the body of Christ united in hierarchical communion. The Second Vatican Council says this when, to the words quoted above, it adds: «Through this sense of faith, which the Spirit of truth inspires and maintains, the People of God, guided in everything by the Magisterium, which they faithfully follow, receive not only the word of men, but truly the word of God (cf. 1 Thes 2:13), unfailingly adheres "to the faith entrusted once for all to the saints" (Jds 3), he penetrates more deeply into it with accurate judgment and applies it more fully to life” [16]. Without a doubt, the faithful, who also participate, to a certain extent, in the prophetic mission of Christ[17], contribute in many ways to increasing the understanding of faith in the Church. «In fact, as the Second Vatican Council says, understanding grows both of the realities and of the words transmitted when the faithful contemplate and study them, meditating on them in their hearts (cf. Luke 2:19.51), when they intimately perceive the spiritual realities they experience, when they are proclaimed by the Bishops, who, with the episcopal succession, received the certain charisma of truth»[18]. The Supreme Pontiff Paul VI also insists that the Pastors of the Church give a “testimony that is firmly linked to Tradition and Sacred Scripture and nourished by the life of the entire People of God”[19]. But only to these Pastors, successors of Peter and the other apostles, does it belong by divine institution to teach the faithful authentically, that is, with the authority of Christ, participated by them in various ways; For this reason, the faithful cannot be satisfied with listening to them as experts in Catholic doctrine, but are obliged to receive what they teach, with adherence proportionate to the authority they possess and intend to exercise[20]. Hence the Second Vatican Council, following in the footsteps of the First Vatican Council, teaches that Christ has instituted in Peter "the perpetual and visible principle and foundation of the unity of faith and communion"[21]; and, for his part, the Supreme Pontiff Paul VI has stated: "The Magisterium of Bishops is for believers the sign and the path that allows them to receive and recognize the word of God"[22]. As much as the sacred Magisterium makes use of the contemplation, life and search of the faithful, however, its function is not limited to sanctioning the consent expressed by them, but even, when interpreting and explaining the written or transmitted word of God, it can prevent such consent and demand it[23]. And, finally, the People of God, so that they do not suffer impairment in the communion of the one faith, within the one body of their Lord (cf. Eph 4:4f), especially need the intervention and help of the Magisterium when within their own midst divisions arise and spread regarding the doctrine that must be believed or maintained.

3. The infallibility of the Magisterium of the Church Jesus Christ wanted the Magisterium of the Pastors, to whom he entrusted the ministry of teaching the Gospel to all his people and the entire human family, to be endowed with the appropriate charisma of infallibility in matters of faith and customs. Since this charisma is not the fruit of new revelations enjoyed by the successor of Peter and the College of Bishops[24], they are not exempt from the need to scrutinize with appropriate means the treasure of divine Revelation contained in the Holy Scriptures, which teaches us without corruption the truth that God wanted to be written for our salvation[25], and also contained in the living Apostolic Tradition[26]. In the fulfillment of their mission, the Pastors of the Church enjoy the providential assistance of the Holy Spirit, which reaches its peak when they instruct the People of God, in such a way that they transmit a doctrine necessarily free of error, by virtue of the promises of Christ made to Peter and the other apostles. This takes place when the Bishops, dispersed throughout the world, but teaching in communion with the successor of Peter, agree to consider a sentence as final[27]. The same thing happens even more clearly when the Bishops, with a collegial act - as in the case of the Ecumenical Councils - in union with their visible Head define a doctrine that there is an obligation to maintain[28], and also when the Roman Pontiff "speaks ex cathedra, that is, when, fulfilling his office as pastor and doctor of all Christians, he defines with his supreme apostolic authority that a doctrine on faith or on customs must be maintained by the Church. universal»[29]. According to Catholic doctrine, the infallibility of the Magisterium of the Church not only extends to the deposit of faith, but also to everything without which such deposit cannot be adequately guarded or exposed[30]. The extension of this infallibility to the very deposit of faith is a truth that the Church from its origins has held to be certainly revealed in the promises of Christ. Relying precisely on this truth, the First Vatican Council defined the object of Catholic faith: "Everything that is contained in the written or transmitted word of God and that the Church proposes to be believed as divinely revealed, with a solemn declaration or through the ordinary and universal Magisterium, must be believed with divine and catholic faith"[31]. Consequently, the objects of the Catholic faith, which are known as dogmas, are necessarily and have been at all times the immutable norm not only for the faith, but also for theological science.

4. Do not minimize the gift of infallibility of the Church From what has been said above about the extent and conditions of the infallibility of the People of God and the Ecclesiastical Magisterium, it follows that in no way are the faithful allowed to admit in the Church only a "fundamental" permanence in the truth, which, as some maintain, can be reconciled with errors scattered everywhere in the sentences that the Magisterium of the Church teaches as definitive, or in what it professes. without a doubt of any kind the People of God in matters of faith and customs. It is true that through saving faith men are converted to God[32], who reveals himself in his Son Jesus Christ; But it is a mistake to want to infer from this that the dogmas of the Church that express other mysteries can be despised or denied. Furthermore, conversion to God, which we are obliged to provide by faith, is a certain obedience (cf. Rom 16:26) that must be adapted to the nature of Revelation and its demands. This Revelation, in the entire area of ​​salvation, narrates and teaches that the mystery of God, who sent his Son into the world, must be applied to the conduct of Christians (cf. 1 Jn 4:14); and demands, therefore, that in full obedience of understanding and will to God who reveals[33] the announcement of salvation be accepted as it is infallibly taught by the Pastors of the Church. The faithful are duly converted, through faith, to God, who reveals himself in Christ, when they adhere to Him, in all the doctrine of the Catholic faith. There is certainly an order and a hierarchy of the dogmas of the Church, its connection with the foundation of faith being diverse[34]. This hierarchy means that some dogmas rely on others as more important and receive light from them. However, all dogmas, because they have been revealed, must be believed with the same divine faith[35].

5. Do not corrupt the notion of infallibility of the Church The transmission of divine revelation by the Church encounters difficulties of different kinds. These arise first of all from the fact that the hidden mysteries of God "by their nature so transcend human understanding that, although they have been transmitted by revelation and received by faith, they nevertheless remain veiled by faith itself and as if enveloped in darkness"[36]; and they also arise from the historical conditioning that affects the expression of revelation. With regard to this historical conditioning, it must be observed above all that the meaning of the statements of faith depends in part on the expressive power of the language in a certain time and in certain circumstances. It also happens, not infrequently, that a dogmatic truth is expressed at first in an incomplete, although not false, way, and later, in a broader context of faith and human knowledge, it is expressed in a more full and perfect way. The Church, on the other hand, with its new statements, attempts to confirm or clarify the truths already contained, in one way or another, in Sacred Scripture or in previous expressions of Tradition, but at the same time it is also concerned with resolving certain questions or removing errors; and all this must be taken into account to understand such statements well. Finally, although the truths that the Church wants to teach effectively with its dogmatic formulas are distinguished from the mutable thoughts of an era and can be expressed outside of these thoughts, it may nevertheless be the case that these truths can be enunciated by the sacred Magisterium with terms that contain traces of such conceptions. Keeping all this in mind, it must be said that the dogmatic formulas of the Magisterium of the Church have been suitable from the beginning to communicate the revealed truth and, as long as they are maintained, they will always be suitable for those who interpret them correctly[37]. However, it does not follow from this that each of them has been or will continue to be so to the same extent. For this reason theologians try to establish what exactly the intention of teaching is really contained in the various formulas, and with this work they provide notable help to the living Magisterium of the Church, to which they are subordinate. For this same reason it may also happen that some ancient dogmatic formulas and others related to them remain alive and fruitful in the habitual use of the Church, provided that new expositions and statements are opportunely added to them that preserve and illustrate their primordial meaning. On the other hand, it has also happened from time to time that in this same habitual use of the Church some of these formulas have given way to new expressions that, proposed or approved by the sacred Magisterium, manifest their meaning more clearly and fully. Furthermore, the very meaning of the dogmatic formulas is always true and consistent with itself within the Church, although it can be clarified more and better understood. It is necessary, therefore, for the faithful to avoid the opinion according to which in principle dogmatic formulas (or some type of them) cannot manifest the truth in a concrete way, but only mutable approximations that deform or alter it in some way; and that the same formulas, furthermore, only indefinitely manifest the truth, which must be continually sought through those approximations. Those who think this way do not escape theological relativism and falsify the concept of infallibility of the Church, which refers to the truth that must be explicitly taught and maintained. An opinion of this type is opposed to the declarations of the First Vatican Council, which, despite being aware of the progress of the Church in the knowledge of revealed truth[38], has nevertheless taught that "the meaning of the dogmas, which our holy mother the Church has proposed once and for all, must be maintained permanently and cannot be abandoned with the vain pretense of achieving a deeper intelligence"[39]; He also condemned the sentence according to which it may happen "that the dogmas proposed by the Church must sometimes be given, according to the progress of science, another meaning different from that understood and understood by the Church"[40]: There is no doubt that, according to these texts of the Council, the The meaning of the dogmas declared by the Church is determined and irreformable. The aforementioned opinion also disagrees with the statement made by the Supreme Pontiff John XXIII about Christian doctrine, at the inauguration of the Second Vatican Council: "It is necessary that this certain and immutable doctrine, to which faithful assent must be given, be studied and expounded in accordance with the demands of our time. In fact, one thing is the deposit of faith, that is, the truths contained in the revealed doctrine, and another thing is the way of expressing these truths while preserving, however, the same meaning and significance. Since the successor of Peter speaks here of the certain and immutable Christian doctrine, of the deposit of faith that is identified with the truths contained in this doctrine, and also speaks of these truths whose meaning cannot be changed, it is clear that he recognizes that the meaning of the dogmas is knowable by us, and is true and immutable. The novelty that he himself recommends, taking into account the needs of the times, concerns only the way of investigating, exposing and enunciating the same doctrine in its permanent sense. In a similar way, the Supreme Pontiff Paul VI, exhorting the Pastors of the Church, declared: "We must apply ourselves today with every effort to preserve in the doctrine of faith the fullness of its meaning and its content, expressing it, however, in a way that speaks to the spirit and heart of the men to whom it is addressed"[42].

6. The Church, associated with the priesthood of Christ Christ our Lord, Pontiff of the new and eternal alliance, has wanted to associate and conform with his perfect priesthood the people rescued by him with his blood (cf. Heb 7:20-22. 26-28; 10:14.21). He has, therefore, made the Church participate in his priesthood through the common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial or hierarchical priesthood; These two forms of the priesthood, which differ essentially and not only in degree, are ordered reciprocally in the communion of the Church[43]. The common priesthood of the faithful, also properly called the royal priesthood (cf. 1 Pet 2:9; Rev 1:6; 5:9ff.), because it brings about the conjunction of the faithful, as members of the messianic people, with their heavenly King, is conferred in the sacrament of baptism. By virtue of this sacrament, by reason of the indelible sign called character, the faithful "incorporated into the Church are destined for the worship of the Christian religion" and, "regenerated as children of God, are obliged to confess before men the faith that they received from God through the Church"[44]. Therefore, all those who have been reborn through baptism "by virtue of their royal priesthood attend the offering of the Eucharist and exercise said priesthood in the reception of the sacraments, in prayer and thanksgiving, through the witness of a holy life, in self-denial and in active charity"[45]. Furthermore, Christ, Head of his mystical Body that is the Church, constituted the apostles and, through them, the Bishops, his successors, ministers of his priesthood, so that they would represent him personally in the Church[46]; These in turn legitimately communicated the sacred ministry received to the priests in a subordinate degree[47]. In this way, the apostolic succession of the ministerial priesthood was established in the Church for the glory of God and at the service of the entire human family, which must be led towards God. By this priesthood, Bishops and priests "are segregated in a certain way within the People of God, but not to be separated either from the people themselves or from any man, but to consecrate themselves totally to the work for which the Lord assumes them"[48], that is, to the function of sanctifying, teaching and governing, the exercise of which is concretely determined by hierarchical communion[49]. This multiform function has as its principle and foundation the uninterrupted preaching of the Gospel[50], and has as its summit and source of the entire Christian life the Eucharistic Sacrifice[51], which the priests, as representatives in person of Christ the Head, in his name and in the name of the members of his mystical Body[52], offer to the Father in the Holy Spirit; and which is later integrated into the Holy Supper in which the faithful, participating in the one body of Christ, all become one body (cf. 1 Cor 10:16f). The Church has increasingly investigated the nature of the ministerial priesthood, which since apostolic times has been constantly conferred through a sacred rite (cf. 1 Tim 4:14; 2 Tim 1:6). With the assistance of the Holy Spirit, he has gradually achieved the clear persuasion that God has wanted to show him that that rite confers on the priests not only an increase of grace to holily fulfill the ecclesial functions, but also imprints a permanent seal of Christ, that is, the character by virtue of which, endowed with an appropriate power derived from the supreme power of Christ, they are enabled to fulfill those functions. The permanence of character, whose nature is otherwise explained variously by theologians, is taught by the Council of Florence[53] and is confirmed in two decrees of the Council of Trent[54]. Lately, this permanence has also been recalled on several occasions by the Second Vatican Council[55], and the second general Assembly of the Synod of Bishops has precisely considered that the existence of the priestly character, which remains throughout life, belongs to the doctrine of faith[56]. This stable existence of the priestly character must be admitted by the faithful and must be taken into account for a correct judgment on the nature of the priestly ministry and on the corresponding modalities of its exercise. Regarding the power proper to the ministerial priesthood, the Second Vatican Council, in accordance with sacred Tradition and numerous documents of the Magisterium, has taught: "Although anyone can baptize believers, it is nevertheless the responsibility of the priest to bring to completion the edification of the Body through the Eucharistic sacrifice"[57]; and further: «The same Lord, in order that the faithful would form a single body, in which "not all the members perform the same function" (Rom 12:4), constituted ministers from some of the faithful, who in the society of believers would enjoy the sacred power of Order to offer the Sacrifice and forgive sins»[58]. Likewise, the second general Assembly of the Synod of Bishops has rightly affirmed that only the priest, as a representative of Christ in person, can preside and perform the sacrificial banquet, in which the People of God is associated with the oblation of Christ[59]. Without wanting to enter now into the questions about the minister of each of the sacraments, according to the testimony of sacred Tradition and the sacred Magisterium, it is evident that the faithful who, without having received priestly ordination, took upon themselves the function of performing (conficiendi) the Eucharist, would try to do something that, in addition to being seriously illicit, would also be invalid. And it is evident that abuses of this type, if they exist, must be repressed by the Pastors of the Church. * * * The present declaration has not attempted, nor was it its purpose, to demonstrate by a proper study of the foundations of our faith, that divine Revelation has been entrusted to the Church to maintain it unaltered in the world. But this dogma, which constitutes the very origin of the Catholic faith, has been remembered, along with other truths that concern the mystery of the Church, so that it appears clearly, in the current confusion of ideas, what is the faith and doctrine that the faithful must firmly profess. The Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith is glad that theologians apply themselves diligently to investigate the mystery of the Church. He also recognizes that his work frequently addresses questions that can only be clarified through complementary research and on the basis of attempts and conjectures. However, the just freedom of theologians must remain within the limits of the word of God, as it has been faithfully preserved and expounded in the Church, and as it is taught and explained by the living Magisterium of the Pastors, first of all, of the Shepherd of all the People of God[60]. The same Sacred Congregation entrusts this declaration to the attentive request of the Bishops and of all those who, by whatever title, share the duty of safeguarding the deposit of truth entrusted to the Church by Christ and his apostles. And he also addresses it with confidence to the faithful and in a special way, given the importance of their role in the Church, to priests and theologians, so that everyone is in agreement in the faith and sincerely feels with the Church. The Supreme Pontiff, by divine Providence Pope Paul VI, in the Audience granted to the undersigned Prefect of the Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, on May 11, 1973, has ratified and confirmed this Declaration on Catholic doctrine about the Church to defend it from some current errors, and has ordered its publication. Given in Rome, at the Headquarters of the Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, on June 24, 1973, feast of Saint John the Baptist. FRANJO Card.
